item.content:encoded:
I'm glad to hear it! :D

Her parents didn't name her Aé, but she doesn't really remember her parents, so Aé is what she named herself. Aé has always been what I called this character; I was a bit in love with random generators at the time and have always been a sucker for vowels.

My earliest versions of her actually had an even more cliche backstory, on account of my having been, like, 14 or something when I first made her. Basic last-of-her-village tragic past with a weeaboo species name, this one specific reed species that's slime-immune purely as a handwave to make her fully-dressed because clothes are just mandatory, etc. She was a basic mediocre learning-to-write OC, except with weird biology stuff going on because even then I had the urge to Write Weird Stuff. I just didn't have the skill or setting to make her usable in freeform forum RP, so I ended up retiring her. Five years later, when I changed her backstory and circumstances to make her an SCP, I changed her personality accordingly, but I don't remember what proto-Aé's personality was. It was probably really generic.

I feel very fortunate that Aé was finally able to find her home here.

How did I only just now see this? I love her. This is a great article to demonstrate the Foundation's more caring side, which is absolutely fantastic because the writing remains so clinical throughout. The containment procedures almost remind me of instructions/warnings on medications. You perfectly nailed the tone and, in my opinion, the whole "feel" of the SCP Foundation— normal enough to go mostly unnoticed, kind of cool, kind of Existentially Wrong/Bad, kind of creepy— without falling too much into one attribute to the detriment of another. And while the "morally dubious scientist injecting small child with ??? substance and making them Not Human" backstory might be a little cliched, I think it fits within the universe of the Foundation.

Meta question: has her name always been Aé, or has it changed since her inception? Has she always had this backstory and these specific character traits?

Also, I love how you incorporate disabled staff and accommodations for them, that's hella rad and something I'd love to see more in other articles.

I mean, this is legit so good I dusted off my old account just to write a pointlessly-long comment and give it an upvote.

item.content:encoded:
The purpose of special containment procedures is to assure safety for both the SCP object and anyone handling it. Currently, the shortest person who might plausibly enter the containment area is only a meter tall. Just because there happens to only be one person that height at the workplace doesn't make them exempt from workplace safety considerations.

The reason researcher-specific procedures are discouraged is because having to go to Dr. So-and-So in the event of X or to approve Y is that, if Dr. So-and-So dies, the procedure stops working. If Dr. Trebuchet dies or is reassigned, the safety of the maximum water depth isn't compromised. It would just mean that someone might non-urgently consider updating the procedures

Let's look at the options:

The maximum water depth is height X.

A simple statement of a set number that anyone can follow.

The maximum water depth is half the height of the shortest person assigned to SCP-811.

A conditional statement that requires every person reading the document to know who the shortest person assigned to SCP-811 is, know how many centimeters tall that person is, and then do arithmetic on the fly to determine the maximum safe water depth. This is not safe.

The maximum water depth is height X, unless Dr. Trebuchet dies or is reassigned, in which case the maximum water depth is height Y.

This is an if/then statement that passive-aggressively singles out a member of staff by name for having a disability that needs accommodations. This is not professional or appropriate.

The maximum water depth is height Y.

A simple statement of a set number that anyone can follow, but following it creates a situation in which a Foundation employee is at undue risk of drowning. This is also not safe.

item.content:encoded:
If I rewrote SCP-811 today, I'd probably replace the syringe-wielding villain origin with something less generic, like: A kidnapper with much more mundane motives went into the swamp with her to hide from authorities, and they stumbled into a spatial anomaly where the air felt wrong in some way she couldn't put a finger on and they got lost and kept going in circles. and she got hungrier and hungrier until she felt an explosion of pain and keeled over puking her blood and organs out. The kidnapper tried to ditch her and run but kept finding himself back in the same place over and over until she got up and ate him. The moment he died, the strange feeling in the air lifted and she was back in the non-anomalous swamp, but she had fully transformed at that point. It's left ambiguous where or with whom the anomaly originated, but the Foundation hasn't been able to replicate it with only adults and the Ethics Committee won't let them have D-classes march actual children through a swamp for hours to see if they turn into monsters.

EDIT 1/17/19: If I rewrote SCP-811 today, I'd probably add something about a compound isolated from her not-blood that, when injected, successfully turns young mice into 811 instances that only ooze digestive mucus when it's feeding time and, like most mice, are mostly scavengers. It kills adult mice and adult humans by incomplete transformation. To Dr. Trebuchet's relief, the Ethics Committee refuses to allow testing on human children. I know that doesn't actually do much to expand on the guy's motives or what he thought he was going to accomplish, but I think it'd be a nice touch that might give more insight into what he expected to happen.

Too late to make a change that big now, though.

item.content:encoded:
Thanks! SCP-811 wasn't designed with a specific pre-existing monster in mind. I was fourteen and just messing with the idea of "swamp monster person" or something like that when I first made the character. I've always been a bit of a biology nerd, and so I — being a 14-year-old with little foresight in my writing — did all the Interesting Biology stuff first, and found myself with a character who's completely unusable in pretty much any freestyle forum RP setting because anything she touches that doesn't rot in her hands is still going to have a biohazardous slime stuck on it.

So she gathered dust in my mental Box of Characters I Don't Use for years, until I found the SCP Foundation wiki, and its setting where Aé being Too Weird To Work was actually a good thing, and she's been SCP-811 ever since. The article's gone through a lot of changes over the past eight years, though, and looking back at some of the earlier iterations feels kind of embarrassing for me now.

item.content:encoded:
I really enjoy this one. While it has a somewhat classic/cliché 'creepy monster' vibe to it, the development over the course of the article into something more is just superb. Going from the detail of the monster, to the hints that it's more than a monster, and the interview log, I feel, really seals the deal.

I especially like how Trebuchet handles the conversation. He's familiar with how to interact with 811, to the point where he can even parse the half-speech she uses to dig the right concepts out of it, and parse more complex concepts back to her in a way she understands.

This article, I feel, is one of the best examples of how the Foundation should be handling SCPs: you interact with them as their needs demand. If calling her by a simple name to her face makes it easier to interact with her, do it - there's no problem there. If she's not a problem and makes simple requests that make her easier to manage, do it - there's no problem there. The Foundation needs to have the capacity for cold, clinical distance…but it doesn't make sense for that to be their ONLY approach towards their goal.
